narrative: This week's fire coverage is anchored by a Global Change Biology synthesis arguing that the global fire crisis stems from compounding human and bioclimatic drivers, alongside work showing hostile post-fire thermal conditions shrink activity windows for reptiles and a Holocene reconstruction in which topography shaped boreal fire regimes. On climate, mountain flora in Europe face compositional change in a warming world, while new analyses show that drought metrics can bias estimates of ecosystem water limitation and that root-zone drought risks to rainfed crops are intensifying. Movement and behaviour papers highlight connectivity predicted from step-selection trajectories, planted woodlands that boost functional connectivity across taxa, lizards that actively regulate ultraviolet exposure, and mammals whose avoidance behaviour tracks human presence rather than buildings. Symbiosis studies show trees shifting between root-based foraging and mycorrhizal outsourcing as stand development alters nutrient limitation, and landscape work links connectivity and configuration to alien plant invasions. Conservation and methods items include evidence of strong taxonomic bias in extinction-risk assessment for Antarctic species, a machine-learning app for detecting wildlife trade, and a Python package that opens bioacoustic deep-learning models to wider use, while Nature Ecology and Evolution reports that global biodiversity models perform poorly at local scales.
